title: Sila Paramita
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny takes up sila, the paramita of ethics, as the second in a series on the six paramitas, tracing it to right speech, right action, and right livelihood in the Eightfold Noble Path. Reizan describes the path as a wheel, notes that Theravada students begin with ethics before meditation, and favors guidelines as touchstones over moral absolutism, always imagining oneself slightly off the mark and working toward it. Reizan then opens a discussion on living ethically in a turbulent time, where participants offer listening, Suzuki Roshi's shining one corner of the world, and a friend's daughter who answers her angry brother by asking, "What would happen then?"

Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagatas.
Good evening everyone.
Now I see what it's like for Tim.
This is very odd, because here in my room I'm just talking to myself.
I don't hear ums and ahs and laughter, or I don't even hear people saying hi when I say hi.
So I'll just imagine you're all there, which I see, and apologies for any fumbling there.
We are giving a series of talks this month on the six paramitas, and I believe this is the second talk as we're doing them in order.
This is a talk on sila, which is the paramita of morality or conduct ethics.
The paramitas are a formulation of Buddhist teaching that draws on earlier formulations of Buddhist teachings.
One of the earliest formulations was the Eightfold Noble Path.

To review, the Eightfold Path is right view or outlook, right thought or intention, right speech or expression, right action or conduct, right livelihood, work or reliance, right effort or constancy, right mindfulness or awareness, and right concentration, samadhi or meditation.
I think it's instructive to look back at that as a ground for talking about sila, perhaps in particular, and perhaps for some of the other paramitas.

Because sila essentially comprises a third or a one-third piece of those eight, the Noble Eightfold Path, which was traditionally seen as a collection that could be divided into three groups: morality, concentration, and wisdom.
Wisdom, in this sense, is simply the eighth step of the path, and concentration being, and perhaps in some ways viewed even as the first step of the path.
The Eightfold Path was sort of seen as being, even in some ways, circular.

It was often depicted as a circular, a dharmic wheel with eight spokes, and that was a predominant symbol in early Buddhist times, at a time when it wasn't thought of as being appropriate to actually show a physical depiction of the Buddha as a whole.
That was a symbol of the eightfold path.
Right speech, right action or conduct, and right livelihood are all of the same things.
The Eightfold Path, in this sense, is often seen as a wheel with eight spokes, and right speech, right action or conduct, and right livelihood are all of the same things.
The Eightfold Path, in this sense, all seem collectively as being part of sila.
This wasn't some new concept that the Buddha came up with; it was drawn out of earlier teachings, the idea of ideas of conduct, systems of ethics and morality.
By nature, it would seem appropriate that that would be somehow incorporated into how Buddhists viewed ethics or morality.
The Eightfold Path was sort of progressive in a sense.

Right view was just the stance that you took towards the world, the sort of attitude that you brought, or just the sort of awareness or belief or viewpoint from which you came from, sort of before you've really dealt with anything or even thought about it—just where you're coming from.
Then right thought, right intention, the idea of that thought is then coming out of that right viewpoint; it's arising.
Right speech would then be an expression of that thought, and right action would be an action based on your words.
Right livelihood or reliance would be how you sort of run your life, your lifetime of actions, and how that sort of constructs the life you live.
Right effort or constancy would be your effort to maintain this correctness to the way you live, which would involve right mindfulness, being aware at all times how you're doing with this.
This would naturally lead to right concentration or meditation, which by virtue of the process of meditation would then help arise again, right views.
So this would be a circular process.
In many schools of Buddhism, especially in the Theravadan tradition, believed that Sila was the foundational practice.
A new student wouldn't be brought to the cushion, as they might in a Zen setting first.
They would be asked instead to take upon themselves a small course in ethics to sort of correct the ship of their life, clean up their act a little bit, get their life centered.
From that center, then the ground of meditation can be entered in truthfully and productively.
In the Buddhist tradition, it wasn't just seen as being an idea of a negative expression.
In other words, don't lie as an expression of right speech, or it would be also expressed positively, as in speak truthfully or speak kindly.
That sort of relates a little bit to just how the entire idea of ethics or morality can be dealt with in a human life.
There's sort of a scale, I suppose, of whether we're talking about an idea of moral absolutism or moral relativism.

Is this something that a set of qualities that we're working on, that we're holding in front of ourselves as a teaching example to touch back with as we go through our actions of our days and use as guideposts, so to speak, sort of moral relativism?
Or is it a moral absolutism?
Is there something absolutely right and wrong that if you've done it, you're wrong and that's going to mark you?
If you've done it the other way, you're right and that's going to mark you?
And there's an absolutism about what is right and what is wrong in life.
I think we've seen expressions across the scale of all of that in the way the idea of ethics can be presented.
I think that a lot of us coming from religious contexts feel that the idea of morality is we're familiar with an absolutist conception of it.

Even if we disagree or feel uncomfortable with that moral absolutism, it still forms the core of our basic feeling about it because we've lived a life where a lot of moral absolutism got laid down on us in various ways.

So some people will then really want to run away from the idea of a moral system, any kinds of do's and don'ts, because the idea of an absolutist presentation of that is so off-putting that they need to separate from that.
That's understandable, and it's understandable for me.
But the moral relativism of just having a set of guidelines to help be a touchstone to life is much more attractive to me.
It's something that I've found to be reflective, at least in the way Zen practice has been conveyed from teachers I've worked with, with Norman and others.
So it's really a situation of working on it and continuing to work on it, which brings up the idea of whether we feel we're doing any good at that.
Most of the time we don't feel we're doing a good job.
That just seems to be our basic attitude about ourselves by and large.
Sometimes we don't even think we're doing an acceptable job, and we're often constantly trying to figure out how to act in any given moment.
Something comes up and we're thinking, what's the right thing?
What's the wrong thing?
This is something that can set us.
If we take on an ethical practice, it can be a burden.

It can be an idea of like, I told myself I was going to be thinking about these important right and wrong things, and now I'm constantly, this is going through my mind almost, I just must not be doing this good.
I must not be doing well at this at all.
A lot of times we just imagine we're faking it.
And even when somebody else says, you did a really good job, we're the ones who think, yeah, I could have done better, and we believe that.
And actually, that's true.
We always can do better because we never really are on the mark about anything.
I think that one of the things to think about is that if we think we're on the mark, we're probably just feeling overconfident and missing something.
I think it's better to, in our practice of pursuing our ethical practice, to always imagine ourselves as being just slightly off the mark and always working towards where we need to be.
Because that working towards attitude is the attitude of being in ethical alignment with our practice.
It's not really so much about whether we get it right or get it wrong.
It's, are we working towards it?
And when we are working towards it, because that's more the nature of our life, then in that way, we kind of are perfect.
We think we're not doing any good and maybe we're not feeling like we really have a handle on some of the precepts or some of the ethical practices.
But if we have that in mind and we're bringing it up in mind and we're adjusting our actions based off of just a good intention, then we're perfect.
That's really the best we can do, right?
And if you're doing the best you can do, well, that has to be perfect, right?
So this brings up the whole thing about right and wrong.

I was hoping here at the end to maybe just open this up and have a little discussion to talk about, in a world gone topsy-turvy where what is right and wrong and true and false seem constantly in debate, where we see what we consider wrong to be happening everywhere.
What do we do with a practice of ethics?
How do we view our own guilt or inability to do what we believe is right at any time?
Or how do we feel we're doing well enough, or even how do we know that we were doing well enough in this practice?
What can our practice of trying to maintain good speech, maintain good actions, maintain a good livelihood do?
How does it work in a time when all around us we feel the ground of that kind of work is just pulled out from underneath us?
Which, at least for me, I sort of feel that that's my feeling about society in these days.
And so anyway, I'm interested to hear what other people might have to say about this.
I think I've talked enough.
Could you unmute us?
And maybe we'll do a little, people can chime in, raise a hand or chime in as you want, or unmute yourself as you want.
I find this is a time to listen and observe and wait.
I'm fortunate, as I hope we all are, to have a safe place to live.
I have food, shelter, and I don't understand what's going on.
I can't feel good about it.
Bad bad things are happening.
But I know there's a larger context that I probably I'm not aware of.
There's a lot of conditions that I don't know about.
And this is a time of great, silent waiting for me.
And I feel that that's an ethical stance because I'm not out harming others or myself, except incidentally, as that may happen, but certainly not intentionally.
So practice not knowing, and maybe having developing faith that this is an evolutionary, revolutionary time, and just see what goes.
That's how I'm doing.
I think it's notable, listening to what you're saying about inaction is really inaction is a type of action.
Your question reminded me of a little, I think it's a Suzuki Roshi quote that I liked about shining one corner of the world.
And I think how we treat the people we live with and our neighbors and just the people we encounter in day to day life does matter.
It might not affect the big world picture or anything like that, but our small lives in this little corner of the world, we can be kind, we can be patient, we can be generous.
We can try to make a small difference, and that matters.
So I tell myself that.
I think Lee's point about listening, that's always good advice to be a good listener.

And yeah, I'm actually kind of hopeful that some of the big disturbances we're having now, the protests and a real emphasis on noticing the racism that's been in this culture for a long, long, long time, maybe something will come out of that.
I'm hopeful.
We'll see.
But in the meantime, just to pay attention to our little day to day lives, that matters.
Hey, Ken?
You know, I'm just struck by the fact that ethics and upright living is inherently an intensely personal thing.
The world can be topsy-turvy, but everything about ethics is how you act personally and how you react to things that you run into.

To a degree, the most I can hope for in crazy times like this is that I manage to maintain my own ethics, and that in doing so, if myself and enough like-minded people act that way, one ant can't move a building, but if you have a million ants, you can do a whole lot of stuff.
So I just think it's additive, but each of us is responsible ourselves.
Jeff and I kind of got into an ethical discussion.
We went into a meal with a group of folks outside; we were all socially distanced.
There's a couple that often joins us, and they're not of the same political persuasion that we are.
We've been doing this for years now, we just don't talk about it.
But Jeff did get into a discussion with the fellow, and then I had to start bumping his leg, and then it got heated.
They were talking about defunding the police, and they both were taking different positions.
I was thinking, oh man, this family gathering is falling down the tubes.
When we got home, I was urging him to just listen.
Could you not just listen?
His position was that he's misinformed, and it's his responsibility to speak the truth in this situation.
I can throw that out to all of you.
I still feel, particularly in a situation like that, that it's better just to listen.
If there's a door opening and you feel like you can express your opinion, but at the same time, keep that door open, do that.
But these people have a different mind.
I don't know how other people feel about that.
Is it important?
Should we be talking to people about our differences, even when it creates tension?
I think that is where discernment comes in.
I cannot say yes or no to that question for myself.
I confess, being of a Central European background, I'm probably a bit more blunt than most people are.
I put my views out there when it is making a difference.
Just arguing with someone, for myself at least, just arguing with someone doesn't change anybody's mind.

However, when I really think that it needs to be said, and I would not like to be quiet and let the train run away, sometimes it's important to say no when someone expresses overt racism; I'm going to jump in and burn my nose.
Or if someone expresses something that is really hostile to life and well-being of other people, I say something, and I try to be smart about how and what I say.
I probably don't say everything I want to say, but I think it's not a yes or no thing; it's so situational.
Thank you.
Hey, Jeff.
Hi, Scott.
A bunch of years ago, I was trying to make a personnel decision about another member, and I ran up against a word called ethics.
It dawned on me at that point that my generation must have been about the first generation where I wasn't taught in school.
So I got into some books and started reading.
It didn't get too much further than doing the golden rule—doing others or the greatest good for the greatest number, or can't do those things that you want others to do.
But it didn't really answer the question.
So I kind of had to go into it myself.
What I finally decided was that, like some people were saying, it is to listen respectfully, which is extremely hard for me; it takes a lot of practice.
But the other part of that is to stay in the moment.
If I stay in that exact moment and then listen to what is being said or appraising the situation, I don't bring an awful lot of prejudices and prior ideas into the situation.
The third part of that is an idea of my actual import.
The only thing I'm really responsible for is sweeping my side of the street.

So I found that if I walk into a situation where there's a discussion going on, and I keep those three things in mind, an awful lot of, not a lot of the time, I can have a pretty good discussion or problem resolution with somebody where it might have completely gone the way it got the other way.
If I had just said, "Stop, I'm not going to put up with that," I'm not going to put up with that," but I think that's what they talk about when they talk about skillful means.
That's what brings it to mind.
I practice those skillful means to do the greatest, to do good for as many people as I can, and that's it.
Thank you.

Yeah, I think growing up in society where I'm pretty sure that I never voted for anybody for president that won until Barack Obama taught me early on that most people in this country don't agree with me.
So, I figured they're coming from the standpoint that I can be pretty opinionated and more so online.
Have you ever noticed this when you're online?
It's like really easy to let it fly.
But in person, I live out in the county here where I'm a minority political opinion for sure, and I keep it to myself.
In my business acquaintances in the construction world, and my neighbors in the county or whatever, when anything comes up, I just defer to listening as a default mechanism.
I don't think at other times I cannot be a very good listener.
But somehow, in these situations, I'm pretty sure that I'm not going to be heard if I denounce some of these viewpoints straight up.

Mostly, I find that if somebody has a genericized sort of viewpoint that sounds like it got torn out of the headlines, the reason they adhere to that is based off of a personal thing, and you just got to scratch the surface and say, "What do you feel that way?
What example from your life makes this confirmative this idea, like makes sense?"

A lot of times people from another political persuasion, they do have these confirmative life experiences and their real experiences for them, how things are for them, or the realities they've seen or witnessed, that confirm to them that that's the way it is.
It's a much more productive level to talk about your personal experiences than about your beliefs, this high level abstract kind of thing that generally turns into an argument.
Just as an aside, when I bring up a discussion, it's not my philosophy; I try to keep that out of it.
It's like, "How do we move that rock?"
I let the problem and the situation work itself.
A friend of mine told me about her adult son and her adult daughter arguing about stuff, and her son is quite conservative and angry at things, saying the angry statements.
I didn't know what the topic was, but her son would blast out, "Get rid of all those bad people or whatever it was."
And her daughter would say to him, "Well, and then what would happen?"
And then he would go onto another topic.
She said, "Well, then what would happen then?"
And he couldn't answer, so he stopped talking.
I thought that was really brilliant—ask the question, "What would happen then?"
Because that's what we never get to; we get caught in the absurdity of the claim or the explosion or something.
But just ask, "What would happen then?"
She said, "But just ask, well, what happens then?"
If you do that, remember that that's a good thing.
If you get stuck, you can't be quiet; ask what happens next.
Thanks.
Yeah, yeah, I was thinking about that quite a bit.
It seems like on quite a few fronts right now.
It feels like the right thing to do feels so obvious to a group of people, and the opposing, it feels oppositional of the answer to things.
I keep thinking things in terms of winning and losing.
Bob, your idea about voting for that president that never wins, I was thinking about that on a hike: what if what I think should happen and what is the ethical thing and the right thing doesn't win?
I want to win.
I think those ideas are best for people wearing masks will save people's lives.
And what if that doesn't win?

Just that thought of, "Hey, I'm still needing to live that personal ethical way, regardless of whether it wins or loses," gave me this sudden, super freeing feeling, like a weight was kind of lifted off my shoulders of knowing deep in my heart that I'm still going to do the right thing.
But I don't need to beat other people up verbally about that.
Whether or not it turns out in my lifetime that things are going to head in the direction I want to or not, I still have to make those decisions every day.
So I guess it comes down to it's about the means rather than the end.
The way you live your life, right, is the means, is the process of making those choices.
And whether or not we end up with America that it follows its principles and ideals, that's going to be okay.
There'll be people that are going to make good choices, whether it's five people or 300 million.
Let's say it's a rich field of practice, these questions, and keeping them alive, just like this is the way of practicing with them.
I think obviously nobody has a rock-solid answer to any of these questions because anything that you propose is right, if you push it too hard, it ends up being wrong.

Everything has to be taken lightly with a lot of wisdom, a lot of practice, and to keep it right, to keep it kind of within this idea of the Noble Eightfold Path, where there's just this idea of right.
It's not like it almost proposes a situation where you're having to figure out what does it mean by right?
All of a sudden, you're in this inquiring, investigative, perceiving frame of mind towards the subject.
In our series of talks on the six perfections that, Sila, the first of the six is Dhanaparamita.
This idea of a generosity as a foundational practice, of giving as a foundational practice, followed up very closely by ethics as a foundational practice.
We'll continue going forward with exploring the Paramitas, meaning the perfection of these things, which obviously is an endless process.
Well, thanks for the discussion we can do.
May our intention equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Illusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.
